entries.qa: Same word as excuse_me; Israelis use סליחה for most apologies. For a fuller apology: אני מצטער (a-NEE mits-ta-ER), masculine; feminine אני מצטערת (mits-ta-E-ret).
Same word as please; the everyday reply to תודה. Also heard: על לא דבר (al lo da-VAR), אין בעד מה (eyn be-AD ma).
Literally 'in order'. אוקיי (o-KEY) is just as common in casual speech.

The prefix ל (le-) is fixed, but numbers for counting people take masculine forms (לשניים, לשלושה, לארבעה), not the counting forms in vocab. For one person, לאחד is usual for a man (feminine: לאחת). Also common: אנחנו שניים (a-NAKH-noo SHNA-yim, 'we are two').
Also natural: אפשר תפריט? (ef-SHAR taf-REET).

Back-translation: 'I [am] allergic to ___.' Masculine speaker; a woman says אני אלרגית (a-LER-geet). Prefix ל attaches to the allergen word. To stress severity add: זה מסוכן לי (ze me-su-KAN lee, 'it is dangerous for me').
Masculine speaker; feminine אני צמחונית (tsim-kho-NEET). Vegan: טבעוני (tiv-o-NEE).
Back-translation: 'Without ___, please.' בלי never changes form; for an allergy, say allergic_to as well, since בלי alone may be read as a preference.
Literally 'to take'. The standard café answer; טייק אווי is also understood.
Literally 'to sit here'. Pairs with the staff question לשבת או לקחת?
אחד agrees with the item, not the speaker: masculine item (קפה) עוד אחד; feminine item (בירה, כוס) עוד אחת (od a-KHAT).
ל merges with ה: לשדה (li-SDE), לחוף (la-KHOF). In Israel most bus/train fares are paid with a Rav-Kav card, so this is mostly for abroad or intercity counters.
Literally 'Does this arrive to ___?'. Natural on a bus: האוטובוס הזה מגיע ל___? For a train (feminine רכבת): הרכבת הזאת מגיעה ל___? Reviewer: check whether זה נוסע ל___? is preferred.
Masculine addressee (driver); to a woman: תיקחי (ti-ke-KHEE). Many Israelis just say the destination: לשדה התעופה, בבקשה.
Masculine addressee; to a woman: תעצרי (ta-ats-REE). אפשר לעצור פה? (ef-SHAR la-a-TSOR po) is gender-neutral.
Review edit: names the bus, since "the next one" alone sounds unnatural. For a train (רכבת, feminine): מתי יוצאת הרכבת הבאה? (ma-TAI yots-ET ha-ra-KE-vet ha-ba-A).
Direction form ('to the left'). The adjective/side is שמאל (smol).
Direction form ('to the right'). Not 'correct' (that is נכון).
Also heard: ישר ישר (keep going straight).
Literally 'I went to loss'. Past tense, same for men and women.
זה קרוב לפה? (le-PO) is equally common.
Stress on וויי-פיי varies (WAI-fai / wai-FAI). Some say לאינטרנט (la-IN-ter-net) instead.
Uses the English loan צ'ק-אאוט, which Israeli hotels use. Reviewer: check spelling/respelling of the loanword.
Uses מזוודות (suitcases); for backpacks/smaller bags: התיקים (ha-tee-KEEM).

Verb agrees with the noun: masculine עובד (o-VED), feminine עובדת (o-VE-det), plural עובדים (ov-DEEM). For a construct noun the ה moves to the second word. Hot water is more natural as אין מים חמים ('there is no hot water').
Masculine speaker; feminine אני רק מסתכלת (mis-ta-KE-let).
שקית is a plastic/carrier bag (often charged for). Not תיק (handbag/backpack).
Literally 'just to shorten a little'. Reviewer: check against barber usage; רק לסדר (rak le-sa-DER, 'just tidy it') is also common.
Said while showing the photo. כמו בתמונה (kmo ba-tmu-NA, 'like in the picture') is a clearer alternative.
Literally 'to tidy the beard, please'. Reviewer: check; לקצר את הזקן (shorten) is the alternative.
Back-translation: 'Save [me]!' / 'Rescue!' The standard shout for help, said the same by anyone. Israel emergency numbers: police 100, ambulance (Magen David Adom) 101.

Back-translation: '(You all) call to the police!' Plural, addressed to bystanders, same for any gender. To one man: תתקשר (tit-ka-SHER); to one woman: תתקשרי (tit-kash-REE). Police number in Israel: 100.
Back-translation: 'I need a doctor.' Masculine speaker; feminine אני צריכה (tsree-KHA). If urgent: אני צריך אמבולנס (am-bu-LANS), number 101.
Back-translation: 'Where [is] the pharmacy?' בית מרקחת is the standard word; many Israelis just say סופר-פארם (the main chain) or ask איפה יש פה בית מרקחת? ('where is there a pharmacy here?').
Back-translation: 'This is an emergency case.' Shorter and very common: זה דחוף! (ze da-KHOOF, 'it's urgent!').
Back-translation: 'I lost the ___ of mine.' Past tense, same for men and women. ה goes on the noun; for a two-word noun (room key) it becomes את המפתח של החדר שלי.
Back-translation: 'I don't feel good.' Masculine speaker; feminine אני לא מרגישה טוב (mar-gee-SHA).
Back-translation: 'I need to call to someone.' Masculine speaker; feminine צריכה (tsree-KHA). To borrow a phone: אפשר להתקשר מהטלפון שלך? (ef-SHAR le-hit-ka-SHER me-ha-TE-le-fon shel-KHA).
Literally 'Is there to you (plural) ___?'. Plural לכם is the normal way to ask a shop, café or hotel. To one person: יש לך (le-KHA to a man, LAKH to a woman). The noun goes in bare, no article.
Verb agrees with the item: masculine עולה (o-LE), feminine same spelling but said o-LA, plural עולים (o-LEEM). Indefinite items are bare; definite ones take ה (החדר).
Back-translation: 'I need ___, please.' Masculine speaker; feminine אני צריכה (tsree-KHA). Noun goes in bare.

Literally 'Is there here ___ in the area?'. Chosen because nothing agrees with the noun. Alternative יש ___ קרוב? needs קרובה (kro-VA) for feminine nouns. Reviewer: check naturalness vs. יש ___ באזור? (ba-e-ZOR).
The preposition is inside the blank because it changes: ב for cash/card (במזומן, בכרטיס), עם for a phone (עם הטלפון). Gender-neutral.
Literally 'Is it possible to ___, please?'. Same gender-neutral אפשר + infinitive structure as the vetted help_me / say_again / speak_slowly. The blank takes an infinitive verb phrase, not a noun.
Adds בבקשה, as the vetted i_would_like does; bare אני רוצה sounds blunt. רוצה is spelled the same for both genders but a woman says ro-TSA. בלי never changes.
Literally 'Is it possible to ___ here?'. Blank takes an infinitive; gender-neutral. כאן (kan) is a more formal synonym of פה.
Masculine speaker; feminine אני מחפשת (me-kha-PE-set). The object marker את is inside the blank: definite objects take את ה (את היציאה), indefinite ones are bare (מסעדה).

Adjective agrees with the noun: masculine כלול (ka-LOOL), feminine כלולה (klu-LA), plural כלולים (klu-LEEM). The noun takes ה. Also common: זה כולל ___? (ze ko-LEL, 'does it include ___?'), which never changes.
Literally 'Where is it possible to ___?'. Blank takes an infinitive; gender-neutral.

word_metro_station.qa: Israel has no metro yet (Tel Aviv has a light rail: הרכבת הקלה); מטרו is understood for abroad.

word_beach.qa: Israelis often say הים (ha-YAM, 'the sea') for going to the beach.

word_supermarket.qa: Short for סופרמרקט, the everyday word.

word_bag.qa: Handbag/backpack (for lost_my). A shopping/carrier bag is שקית (sa-KEET).

word_nuts.qa: Back-translation: 'nuts' (tree nuts in general; peanuts are separate, בוטנים).

word_gluten.qa: Back-translation: 'gluten'. Gluten-free is ללא גלוטן (le-LO GLOO-ten). Stress: check.

word_shellfish.qa: Back-translation: 'fruits of the sea' (seafood). Covers shellfish; not kosher, so rarely on kosher menus.

word_meat.qa: Back-translation: 'meat'. Note chicken (עוף) is often not thought of as בשר; say בלי בשר ובלי עוף if needed.

word_dairy.qa: Back-translation: 'milk products'. Menus mark this as חלבי (kha-la-VEE).

word_peanuts.qa: Back-translation: 'peanuts'. Snacks like Bamba are peanut-based.

word_one.qa: Counting forms (feminine), as used when counting or reading numbers. Counting people or masculine nouns uses אחד, שניים, שלושה, ארבעה, חמישה... (see table_for examples).

word_card.qa: You will very often hear אשראי (ash-RAI, 'credit') instead.

i_need.qa: Back-translation: 'I need help, please.' Masculine speaker; feminine צריכה (tsree-KHA). In real danger shout הצילו! instead; ambulance 101, police 100.
Most Israelis order taxis by app (Gett); to a hotel desk: אפשר להזמין לי מונית? (ef-SHAR le-haz-MEEN lee mo-NEET).

Literally 'Is it possible to photograph here?'.
Literally 'Can [one] charge the phone here?'; Hebrew says 'the phone' rather than 'my phone'. Word order: פה before the object.

is_included.qa: מע״מ = VAT, the tax people ask about in Israel. Foreign tourists are often exempt from VAT on hotel stays.
Uses מזוודה ('suitcase', feminine). Airlines say כבודה (kvu-DA, 'baggage'): הכבודה כלולה? Reviewer: check which reads more naturally for a flight booking.
